reader.title: Reported lynching of A. J. Morris
bases: Wire briefs reported that a mob captured A. J. Morris, accused of murdering Brusher, and hanged him in a saloon (A2, A3, A15), though Kansas reports and a later Beaver City dispatch do not confirm the hanging (A6, A7, A13).

Distant wire briefs say a mob hanged Morris for the murder of Brusher (A2, A3, A15), but the Larned dispatch said only 'probably lynched' (A6), a Kansas local item said only that Morris was arrested (A7), and the Beaver City special named the killer as John Clark, who was tried, fined and freed (A13); the killing itself is not established.

The hanging appears only in one wire brief reprinted in Dakota, Minnesota and Wisconsin papers (A2, A3, A15); Kansas reports call it rumor or probability (A1, A6) and the later Beaver City dispatch gives a different killer and outcome with no mob (A13).

summary.text: The reported lynching of A. J. Morris was the hanging, reported in wire briefs in February 1888, of a man accused of murdering Eugene Brusher, a Kansas cattleman, at Beaver City in No Man's Land.
According to the brief, a mob captured Morris and hanged him to a rafter in the principal saloon of the town.

Kansas papers closer to the scene said only that Morris had been arrested and "probably" lynched, and a later dispatch from Beaver City named a different killer, John Clark, who was tried and set free.
Brusher, about 28 years old, lived at Walnut City in Rush county, owned considerable property and was in the cattle business.
Other Kansas papers called him a cattleman of Rush Center and the late proprietor of the LaGrande Hotel at Ness City.
In early February he arrived at Dodge City with a man who gave his name as Morris and his residence as Ness City, and the two left together for Beaver City, about sixty miles south.
On a Sunday afternoon M. L. Kramer brought Brusher's body to Dodge City and said he had been shot at Beaver City on Friday, February 3, with Morris the supposed murderer.
A Larned dispatch of February 10 added that Morris had stepped up behind Brusher in a saloon lobby, before several men, and shot him through the head.
Brusher was said to have carried $1,100, none of which was found on his body, and the dispatch reported that Morris "was arrested and probably Lynched."

An earlier report in the Barton County Democrat named the killer as "a man named Marsh," placed the shooting on the road near the state line, and passed on rumors that he had been caught and hung or killed in a saloon.

The wire brief that circulated from February 15 stated that Morris was taken to a saloon and hanged to a rafter "in the presence of a large crowd," and one version dated his capture by the mob to "the 10th."
Brusher's burial at Walnut City was said to have excited "a high degree of indignation."
No report of an inquest into Morris's death or of arrests of any mob members appears in the coverage.
On February 18 a special to the Wichita Eagle from Beaver City reported that Brusher's brother George had come to investigate, befriended the killer, then shot him dead and escaped to Kansas.

The hanging reached readers mainly as a one-sentence item in news-digest columns in Dakota, Minnesota and Wisconsin, including the Union County Courier on February 15 and the Iowa County Democrat's "Criminal" column on February 24.
These briefs stated the hanging as fact and described Morris as the man "who murdered" Brusher, though they printed Brusher's initials as "J. B." or "J. D."

Kansas papers, by contrast, ran longer Larned dispatches under headlines such as "A Kansan Murdered in No Man's Land," dwelling on the victim, the missing money and the burial, and treated the lynching as rumor or probability.
The Beaver City account ran in Kansas as "Brusher Revenged" and "Avenged His Brother," and it made no mention of Morris or a mob.
None of the opened reports gives the race of either man.
The reports disagree on who killed Brusher: Morris in the wire briefs and Larned dispatches, Marsh in the first Barton County Democrat item, and John Clark in the Beaver City special.
They also disagree on the date, with the Larned account giving February 3 and the Beaver City special February 10.

In the Beaver City version Clark claimed the shooting was accidental, a trial returned a verdict of criminal carelessness, and he was fined for disturbing the peace and freed, an outcome that leaves no place for a lynching.
That special is the only report datelined from Beaver City itself and the latest, while the hanging appears only in the wire brief carried by distant papers.

accounts.label: Wire digest brief
accounts.gist: A. J. Morris, who murdered Brusher at Beaver, No Man's Land, was captured by a mob (one version says on the 10th) and hanged to a rafter in the principal saloon before a large crowd.

accounts.label: Larned dispatches
accounts.gist: Brusher was shot from behind in a Beaver saloon lobby on Feb. 3 by his companion Morris, apparently for his money; Morris was arrested and 'probably' lynched.

accounts.label: Barton County Democrat
accounts.gist: A man named Marsh shot Brusher in the back on the way to No Man's Land; rumors said the killer was caught and hung, or killed in a saloon.

accounts.label: Wichita Eagle special from Beaver City
accounts.gist: John Clark shot Brusher on Feb. 10, claimed accident, was tried, fined and freed; Brusher's brother George later killed Clark.

framing.detail: Dakota, Minnesota and Wisconsin papers ran the hanging as a one-sentence item in news digests ('Latest News by Wire', 'Criminal'), calling Morris the man 'who murdered' Brusher.
Kansas papers headlined the murder ('Murdered for Money', 'A Kansan Murdered in No Man's Land') and reported the lynching only as rumor or probability.
The Beaver City special ran as 'Brusher Revenged' and 'Avenged His Brother', centering the brother's revenge killing.

conflicts.note: The Beaver City special does not mention Morris; whether Clark and Morris are the same man is not stated.
